title: How To Keep Your Cool
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that while enthusiasm is a hallmark of great teaching, classroom management calls for a different quality entirely: unshakable calm. He illustrates this with the story of Mercury astronaut Gordon Cooper, who famously fell asleep atop a fueled rocket before launch and later used his composure to manually navigate his capsule to safety after instrument failure. From this and other examples — golfer Annika Sorenstam's emotionless consistency, firefighters' deliberately unhurried pace at emergencies — he distills five strategies for teachers to stay calm under provocation: trusting the classroom management plan to do its job, handling misbehavior with detached, matter-of-fact consistency, adopting a machinelike emotional evenness, moving with purposeful calm rather than rushed urgency, and imagining an audience (a parent, a camera) to encourage measured behavior. He frames staying cool as a skill benefiting both teacher and students.
points: Classroom management calls for calm, detached composure rather than the enthusiasm appropriate to lesson delivery.
Trusting the classroom management plan to handle misbehavior reduces the temptation to react emotionally in the moment.
Handling rule violations with matter-of-fact consistency, similar to a mail carrier delivering mail, removes emotional charge from enforcement.
Imagining an audience (a parent standing behind the student, or a camera broadcasting the interaction) can help a teacher stay measured under pressure.
quotes: While most of his fellow astronauts, vetted for being calm under the most trying conditions, were sweating in their pressurized suits and failing to keep their heart rates under control, Cooper had to be awaken during countdown.

Cooper’s cool-headedness saved his life later in the flight when major mechanical problems disabled his navigational instruments and forced him to make manual calculations to avoid burning up in earth’s atmosphere.
Having faith in your classroom management plan and allowing it to do its job will help you be a picture of cool.
When a student breaks a rule, enforce it with the same matter-of-fact way a mail carrier might deliver your mail.

Showing little emotion, even after a bad shot, Annika crushes her competition with a peaceful smile on her face. She has long been called machinelike and robotic. But this is the most effective mental state for golf—as well as classroom management.
Handling classroom management without getting worked-up and feeling angry or stressed is a great benefit for you and your students.
